title: How to Add Stripe Payments to a React App
description: A complete walkthrough of integrating Stripe into React with the PaymentElement — setup, payment intents, webhooks, testing, and the mistakes that cost real money.

author: MyAppAI Team

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body: Adding payments to a React app is one of those tasks that looks simple and has sharp edges. Stripe's React library handles the hard parts — PCI compliance, card input security, payment method UIs — but the integration still requires a backend, correct webhook handling, and careful testing. This guide covers the full path from zero to accepting real payments.

sections.heading: Architecture: What Goes Where
sections.body:
The critical thing to understand upfront: card details must never touch your server. Stripe's model keeps you out of PCI scope by having the browser communicate card data directly with Stripe. Your server's job is orchestration:

Your server creates a PaymentIntent (the amount, currency, customer) and returns its client secret. Your React app uses that secret with Stripe's prebuilt `PaymentElement` to collect payment details. Stripe processes the payment and notifies your server via webhook. Your server fulfills the order only after verifying the webhook.

If you find yourself sending card numbers to your own API, stop — the integration is wrong.

sections.heading: Backend: Creating the PaymentIntent
Frontend: The Payment Form
Webhooks: The Part Everyone Skimps On
sections.body:
After payment, Stripe sends a `payment_intent.succeeded` event to your webhook endpoint. This — not the frontend redirect — is where you fulfill the order. Browsers close, networks drop, and users navigate away; the webhook is the reliable signal.

```js import express from 'express';

app.post('/api/webhook', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => { const sig = req.headers['stripe-signature']; let event; try { event = stripe.webhooks.constructEvent( req.body, sig, process.env.STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET ); } catch (err) { return res.status(400).send(`Webhook error: ${err.message}`); }

if (event.type === 'payment_intent.succeeded') { const intent = event.data.object; fulfillOrder(intent); // grant access, send email, etc. } res.json({ received: true }); } ); ```

Three webhook rules: verify the signature (as above — never trust unverified events), make your handler idempotent (Stripe may deliver the same event twice; check whether you've already fulfilled before acting), and return 200 quickly — do slow fulfillment work asynchronously so Stripe doesn't time out and retry-storm you.

During development, the Stripe CLI forwards webhooks to localhost:

```bash stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/api/webhook ```

sections.heading: Testing
sections.body:
Stripe's test mode is excellent. Use the test card `4242 4242 4242 4242` with any future expiry and any CVC for successful payments, and the documented test cards for specific failures: `4000 0000 0000 0002` for declines, `4000 0025 0000 3155` for 3D Secure authentication flows.

Test the unhappy paths deliberately: declined cards, authentication-required cards, network failure mid-confirm, and duplicate webhook delivery. Each of these will happen in production; finding out how your code behaves should not be a surprise.

Before going live, run through Stripe's activation checklist in the dashboard, switch to live keys, and make one small real payment yourself — refund it after. There is no substitute for watching real money move through the system once.

sections.heading: Mistakes That Cost Real Money
sections.body:
Trusting client-side amounts. Validate every price server-side against your own catalog. Fulfilling on frontend success. Only the verified webhook should trigger fulfillment. Ignoring idempotency. Double-fulfillment from retried webhooks is embarrassing and expensive. No handling for `requires_action`. Some payments need 3D Secure; `confirmPayment` handles the redirect, but your success page must handle the return correctly. Logging full webhook payloads containing customer data into plaintext logs. Log IDs, not payloads. Forgetting to handle disputes. Set up dispute webhooks and actually read them — the evidence submission window is short.

Payments are one of the few features where "it works on my machine" is genuinely insufficient. Test mode, webhooks with signature verification, idempotent fulfillment, and one real live transaction: do all four and you'll sleep fine.
